Q: Why should text files end with a newline? A:

Why should text files end with a newline?

Because that's the sanest choice to make.

Take a file with the following content,

one\n
two\n
three

where \n means a newline character, which on Windows is \r\n, a return character followed by line feed, because it's so cool, right?

How many lines does this file have? Windows says 3, we say 3, POSIX (Linux) says that the file is crippled because there should be a \n at the end of it.

Regardless, what would you say its last line is? I guess anybody agrees that three is the last line of the file, but POSIX says that's a crippled line.

And what is its second line? Oh, here we have the first strong separation:

  • Windows says two because a file is "lines separated by newlines" (wth?);
  • POSIX says two\n, adding that that's a true, honest line.

What's the consequence of Windows choice, then? Simple:

You cannot say that a file is made up of lines

Why? Try to take the last line from the previous file and replicate it a few times... What you get? This:

one\n
two\n
threethreethreethree

Try, instead, to swap second and third line... And you get this:

one\n
threetwo\n

Therefore

You must say that a text file is an alternation of lines and \ns, which starts with a line and ends with a line

which is quite a mouthful, right?

And you want another strange consequence?

You must accept that an empty file (0 bytes, really 0 bits) is a one-line file, magically, always because they are cool at Microsoft.

Which is quite a crazyness, don't you think?

What is the consequence of POSIX choice?

That the file on the top is just a bit crippled, and we need some hack to deal with it.

Being serious

I'm being provocative, in the preceding text, for the reason that dealing with text files lacking the \n at the end forces you to treat them with ad-hoc ticks/hacks. You always need an if/else somewhere to make things work, where the branch dealing with the crippled line only deals with the crippled line, all the other lines taking the other branch. It's a bit racist, no?

My conclusion

I'm in favour of POSIX definition of a line for the following reasons:

  • A file is naturally conceived as a sequence of lines
  • A line shouldn't be one thing or another depending on where it is in the file
  • An empty file is not a one-line file, come on!
  • You should not be forced to make hacks in your code

And yes, Windows does encourage you to omit the trailing \r\n. If you want a two lines file below, you have to omit the trailing \r\n otherwise text editors will show it as a 3-lines file:

Q: Removing an unused class member slows down program? A:

Your program is a real torture test for the memory system.

You've got an array of 302 (K+2) farly large objects of 4K+4 bytes each (and 4K+8 with the unused head_ member) and iterate over each object performing one computation in each.

    for(int i = 1; i <= K; i++)
        A[i].push_back(A[i-1][j] ^ A[i+1][j]);

The address of A[i].data_[j] is base + i*stride + 4*j, and both the L1 set index and store-load disambiguation only look at the low 12 bits of an address. With stride 0x1004, A[i].data_[j] cache line lands at 4*i mod 4096 (the base + 4*j part is a common constant in the inner loop) the 302 arrays barely move through the low bits at all.

Issue 1 -- L1 set conflicts. Each inner loop iteration touches one cache line in each of the 302 arrays. With a stride 0x1004 (4096+4), those lines' low-12-bit offsets span only 4*302 = 1208 bytes - they crowd into ~19 of the 64 L1 sets, i.e. ~16 lines per set in a 12-way L1 (assuming Alder Lake or newer). The working set (~19 KB) would trivially fit in L1, but associativity conflicts evict lines constantly, so loads that should be L1 hits become L2 hits. With stride 0x1008 the spread doubles (8i, ~38 sets, ~8 lines/set) and just fits 12 ways.

Issue 2 -- 4K aliasing (false store-load dependence). In the inner loop, iteration i loads A[i+1][j] while the store to A[i-1] from two iterations earlier is still in flight. Their address distance is 2*stride − 8:

  • stride 0x1004: 2*0x1004 − 8 = 0x2000 -- an exact multiple of 4096, so the low 12 bits match and the memory pipeline treats every such load as potentially depending on that store. This is worse than a throughput penalty: it serializes the loop, because the store's data came from the previous iteration's loads. This false dependency chain runs through every iteration.

  • stride 0x1008: 2*0x1008 − 8 = 0x2008 -- low bits differ -- no false dependence.

The Fix

Pad the class deliberately instead of relying on an accidental field. 16 extra bytes (stride 0x1010) already beats both versions on my system (i7-12700); stride 0x1040 (one full cache line of low-bit advance per array, cycling through all 64 L1 sets evenly) is the robust choice:

class alignas(64) CyclicArray {

Reference data

To prove my findings, attaching VTune analysis reports with both slow and fast versions side-by-side:

Microarchitecture performance buckets:

Annotated assembly (loop unrolling disabled):

Note - "L2 Bound" in the report is the signal that the data doesn't fit in L1.

One caveat on reading the VTune buckets: with a serializing false dependency, "L2 Bound" cycles and "Store Bound" cycles overlap and the top-down attribution gets murky - the same stalled loads get binned partly as L2 hit latency.

Q: Why can SELECT filter a renamed TIME column but DELETE rejects it? A:

As documented in Delete Data | IoTDB Website, only time is allowed in WHERE clause when you want to delete data.

Data deletion in IoTDB can be achieved using the DELETE statement. You can specify filters based on tags and time to delete specific subsets of data.

The page offers the BNF (Backus–Naur Form) syntax of DELETE statement allowed in IotDB:

...

DELETE_CONDITION:
    SINGLE_CONDITION
    | DELETE_CONDITION AND DELETE_CONDITION
    | DELETE_CONDITION OR DELETE_CONDITION

SINGLE_CODITION:
    TIME_CONDITION | ID_CONDITION

That means the condition used in WHERE clause of DELETE statement can be a series of conditions, and each condition can be either a TIME_CONDITION or ID_CONDITION.

TIME_CONDITION:
    time TIME_OPERATOR LONG_LITERAL

ID_CONDITION:
    identifier = STRING_LITERAL

...

Since you are deleting data by a time scope/range, ID_CONDITION is not the one (and it needs to compare an ID with = 'str' syntax anyway), you can only use the time TIME_OPERATOR LONG_LITERAL syntax.

Q: Ethical crawling of academic websites A:

I run a couple of cheesy little web sites with niche information useful to a few people. I publish them with a community spirit on the theory that "information wants to be free".

I've had to block scrapers because of the myriad low-rent AI scrapers that have been slamming the server I rent to publish them. It breaks my heart: I put my little bit of info out there for people to use.

So, your project and mine are falling victim to this tragedy of the commons. It stinks.

Q: If String is a reference type, what exactly happens when we write String name = "Rahul"? A:

If String is a reference type ...

It is.

... what exactly happens when we write String name = "Rahul";?

Lets break this down:

String name

declares a variable called name with type (in this case, class) String. Then

= "Rahul"

assigns a (reference) value to name. The assigned value is a reference to a String object (i.e. an instance of the class String) that corresponds to the "Rahul" string literal.

Where does the object come from?

The object corresponding to "Rahul" is produced by the Java runtime. At some point during the execution of your program, the Java runtime will create a String object to represents the "Rahul" literal. It is the reference to that object that is assigned to name.

How is it created?

It is not specified how it is created. However, one way to do it would be to put the characters 'R', 'a', 'h', 'u', 'l' into a char array and then use the new String(char, int, int) constructor to form a String.

That String will then be "interned"; see this javadoc.

When is it created?

That is also not specified, but it happens before the assignment.

Since the Java Language Specification guarantees that all instances of the literal (say) "Rahul" in the program will refer to the same object. Therefore, we can also be sure that the object creation only happens once for the entire program's execution. That is, NOT every time the = "Rahul" is executed.

In fact, different versions of Java use different strategies to create String objects corresponding to string literals. Some versions create them eagerly when the class is loaded or initialized, and others create them lazily. But you don't need to understand this to use Java.

Also, why don't we write String name = new String("Rahul"); instead?

Basically because it is inefficient. What that actually does is to create a copy of the String object that denotes the "Rahul" literal. There is no need to create that extra copy.

The String(String) constructor has been deprecated because there is (almost1) no valid use-case in Java for creating a String that is a copy of another one.

1 - The only use-cases I'm aware of are when you are writing code that demonstrates the behavior of Java strings, string literals and interning.

Is "Rahul" actually a String object, and does name actually hold a reference to that object?

Yes, the "Rahul" literal denotes an actual String object.

Yes, the variable name will actually hold a reference to that object ... in the original version without the redundant new String(...) stuff.

And ... it will be the same object every time that the statement is executed.
